transcript.content: Hi, welcome. What brings you in today?

I guess the main thing is… I’ve just kind of stopped caring about everything I used to look forward to. It’s hard to explain without sounding dramatic, but things that used to feel like they were mine, like part of who I was, just don’t pull me in anymore.

Like, I’ve got all my fishing gear still sitting in the garage. Normally I’d be checking it, organizing it, thinking about where to go next, messing with the tackle boxes even when I didn’t have a trip planned. Now I walk past it and it’s like looking at someone else’s stuff. Same with my woodshop. I used to lose hours out there, sanding or cutting or planning some little project, and now even the thought of going out there feels like another chore I’m supposed to do.

And my kids will ask me to play chess, which used to be our thing, and I’ll sit there with them, but I’m not really there. I’m just moving pieces around, going through the motions, trying not to make it obvious that I’m not enjoying it. That’s probably what finally made me feel like I should come in, because it’s not just one thing. It’s like the interest went out of everything.
Did this start after a specific stressful event or major change in your life?

Yeah… I mean, I think so. It wasn’t like one single day where everything just snapped, but it really traces back to when my wife’s health problems started changing everything at home. That’s when life kind of stopped being the way it had been.

It’s been about… a year and seven months now, give or take. I remember because at first I kept telling myself it was just a rough patch, like once we adjusted or got through the next appointment or the next change, I’d feel more like myself again. But it just kept stretching on. The house, the routines, what I had time and energy for — all of it shifted around her being sick, and somewhere in that stretch I just sort of… lost the thread. So yeah, I’d say it started after that major change, and it’s been going on ever since.
For most of the past year and a half, have you felt down or depressed nearly every day?

I’m not totally sure how to answer that cleanly. I mean… I know I haven’t felt right for a long time, and there are a lot of days where I feel pretty low, but “nearly every day” makes me stop and think because I don’t really track it that way.

It’s more like everything has been kind of covered over, if that makes sense. Some days I can function and talk to people and get through what I’m supposed to do, so I don’t know if I would’ve called it depressed in the moment. But if you’re asking whether this heavy, down feeling has been hanging around most of the time… yeah, I think it has. I just don’t know if I can honestly say I’ve paid close enough attention to count the days.
Have these low feelings and loss of interest been going on continuously for two years or more?

Not quite two years, no. It feels like it’s been forever, honestly, but if I’m being accurate, it’s been about a year and seven months.

It started around when my wife’s health problems really changed everything at home. That’s the marker in my head, because before that I still felt like I had some normal parts of my life, and after that everything slowly got rearranged around what was happening with her. So… continuous, yeah, more or less since then, but not a full two years yet.
Have you had thoughts that you would be better off dead, or thoughts of hurting yourself?

Yeah… I have. I don’t like saying that out loud, but yes.

It’s not like I’m sitting there making some detailed plan all the time or anything like that, but there are these moments where the thought just shows up, and it scares me how normal it can feel for a second. Especially on the early drives, when I’m up before everyone else and the roads are quiet and it’s still dark out. I’ll be driving and I’ll catch myself thinking… it would be easier if I just didn’t make it there. Like if something happened and I didn’t have to keep doing all of this.

And then sometimes it goes a step further in my head, like the thought of steering off the road comes up, and that’s the part that really scares me, because it feels too close. I don’t want to say I want to do it exactly, but the thought is there, and it doesn’t feel as distant as I wish it did.
Before this started a year and seven months ago, had you ever gone through another period in your life when you felt depressed or lost interest in things for at least two weeks?

I’m not sure I can give you a clean yes or no on that.

I mean, I’ve had hard stretches before, like anybody, I guess. Times where I was stressed or worn down or not really enjoying much for a bit. But when you say “at least two weeks” and feeling depressed or losing interest in things, I don’t know that I ever thought about it that way before all of this started.

Nothing really stands out in my mind as, like, a clear episode where I would’ve said, “Something is seriously wrong with me,” if that’s what you mean. But I also wasn’t exactly keeping track back then. I probably would’ve just told myself to push through it and go to work and not make a thing of it.

So… I don’t know. I can’t point to a definite earlier period like that.
Has this been making it hard for you to keep up with your work?

Yeah. It has. More than I wanted to admit for a long time.

I’m a construction manager, so there are a lot of moving pieces, and I used to be pretty good at keeping them in my head — schedules, crews, deliveries, inspections, safety stuff, who needs to be where and when. Lately I’ve been missing things I shouldn’t miss. Not just little paperwork things, though there’s been that too. I mean things that can affect deadlines, and honestly some things that could affect safety if somebody else doesn’t catch them.

There was a near-miss at work, and after that I couldn’t really keep telling myself it was just stress or that I was tired and needed to push through. I don’t want to make it sound like I caused some disaster, but it shook me because I thought, “Okay, this isn’t just me having a bad attitude. I’m not tracking things the way I need to be tracking them.”

And at home it’s kind of the same pattern, just in a different way. I’m there physically, but I’m not really… useful the way I used to be. My wife and the kids have to work around me more than they can count on me. That’s hard to say, because I used to be someone people could depend on. Now it feels like everyone’s adjusting to whether I’m going to forget something, or be checked out, or not follow through. So yes, it’s definitely making work harder, and it’s not staying at work either.
Have other people noticed that you’ve been moving or speaking noticeably more slowly than usual?

I’m not really sure. I haven’t had anyone say it to me in those words, like, “You’re moving slower” or “You’re talking slower.”

I know I feel slowed down a lot of the time, but whether it’s something other people can actually see, I don’t know. My wife might notice things before I do, but I can’t think of a specific time where someone pointed it out that way. At work, people have noticed I’m not as on top of things, but that’s not exactly the same as moving or speaking slowly.

So… maybe? But I can’t honestly say yes, other people have noticed that specifically.
Have you had a noticeable drop in your appetite?

Yeah. My appetite’s definitely dropped.

Most days food just doesn’t really… taste like anything. Cardboard is the word that comes to mind. I’ll know I should eat, especially if I’m going to be on a job site all day, but breakfast is easy for me to just skip now. I used to at least grab something, even if it was quick, but lately I’ll just have coffee or nothing and keep moving.

Dinner’s the same kind of thing. My wife will make food, or there’ll be food there, and I’ll sit down with everyone, but I’m more picking at it than eating. It’s not like I’m trying to diet or lose weight. I just don’t feel like eating, and when I do, it doesn’t feel worth the effort half the time.

And I’ve noticed it physically too. My belt’s had to come in a couple notches, and I didn’t set out for that to happen. I almost didn’t pay attention to it at first, but then you keep using a tighter hole on the belt and it’s kind of hard to pretend it’s nothing.
Before this started, was there ever a time in your life when you felt depressed or lost interest in almost everything nearly every day for at least two weeks?

I don’t know that I can point to a clear time like that, no.

I mean, I’ve had rough stretches before — everybody does, I guess — times where work was bad or I was stressed or kind of worn down. But if you’re asking whether there was a period before this where, nearly every day for two weeks or more, I felt depressed or like I lost interest in almost everything… I’m not sure. Nothing is coming to mind that I’d confidently describe that way.

I don’t want to say absolutely never, because memory gets a little fuzzy when you’re trying to compare it to what’s happening now. But I don’t remember anything this persistent or this all-consuming before. This feels different enough that it’s hard for me to match it to some earlier episode.
Have you been feeling tired or like you have very little energy nearly every day?

Yeah. Nearly every day, honestly.

It’s not just normal tired, like after a long day on site. It’s more like I wake up already behind. I’ll get going because I have to, but by midmorning I feel like I’ve already worked a full shift. And that’s before the day has really even gotten started.

Walking the project feels harder than it should. Climbing stairs with the crew, going back and forth across the site, even just standing there trying to keep up with what everyone’s saying — my body feels heavy, like I’m carrying wet concrete around with me. That’s the best way I can explain it. Everything takes more effort than it used to.

And I keep trying to tell myself, you know, “Just push through, you’ve done harder days than this,” but it doesn’t feel like the kind of tired that goes away once I get moving. It just kind of sits there all day.
Have you been having trouble sleeping?

Yeah. Sleep’s been… pretty bad.

The strange thing is I’ll be exhausted by the time I get into bed, like my body feels completely done, and I’ll think, “Okay, at least I’ll pass out tonight.” But then I lie there and my head just won’t shut off. I’ll start running through bills, schedules, what has to happen on the job site the next day, who’s waiting on what, what I forgot to do, all of that. It’s like as soon as the room gets quiet, everything I’ve been trying not to think about shows up at once.

And if I do fall asleep, a lot of times I’m waking up around three or four in the morning. Not even for a clear reason. I just wake up and stare at the ceiling, and then I’m aware of every minute going by until it’s time to get up and drive to the site. I’ll tell myself not to look at the clock, but then I do, and it just makes it worse.

So yeah, I’m in bed, but I don’t feel like I’m really resting much.
Have you been feeling worthless?

Yeah… I have. More than I really want to admit.

It’s not like I walk around saying, “I’m worthless,” exactly, but that’s pretty much what it turns into in my head. I keep thinking I’ve failed everybody — my wife, my kids, the guys at work who are counting on me to keep things moving and keep them safe. And then when anything goes wrong, even something that might not totally be on me, I take it like it proves what I already suspect.

Like if I miss an appointment or forget something at home, I’m not just thinking, “Okay, I made a mistake.” I’m thinking, “Of course you did. You can’t even handle basic stuff.” If there’s a cost overrun on a job, or something slips in the schedule, or somebody flags a safety issue, I go straight to, “This is because I’m not good enough to be in charge.” I know construction always has problems — delays, money issues, things you have to solve as they come up — but lately I can’t see it that way. It all feels personal. Like every problem is evidence that I’m useless.

And then I start thinking everyone would probably be better off if I wasn’t the one responsible. My family, the crew, everybody. Not necessarily that they hate me or anything, but just… that I’m letting them down and they’d do better with someone else. It’s hard to say out loud, but yeah, I’ve been feeling pretty worthless.
Have you ever had a period when you felt unusually up, energized, or irritable compared with your normal self?

I don’t think so. I mean… not in the way you’re asking, I don’t think.

I’ve had days where I’m wound up or on edge, sure, especially if there’s a lot going on at work or something’s falling apart and I’m trying to keep everyone moving. And I can get irritable, probably more than I should. But unusually up or energized, like I’m suddenly a different person or full of energy compared to normal… no, I can’t really say I’ve had that.

If anything, lately it’s been the opposite. I’m trying to think if there was ever a stretch where I felt kind of unstoppable or like I didn’t need to slow down, and nothing really comes to mind. There are busy periods where you just push because the job demands it, but that feels more like pressure than feeling good or energized. So… no, I haven’t noticed anything like that.
Before this current period began, did you ever have a time lasting at least two weeks when you felt depressed or lost interest in most things nearly every day?

I’m… not really sure how to answer that, honestly.

I don’t think I can point to a clear time before this where it was like this for two full weeks, where I was depressed or didn’t care about most things nearly every day. I mean, I’ve had rough stretches, sure — everybody does, I guess — times where work was stressful or I was tired or not myself for a while. But if you’re asking whether there was a definite period before now that felt like this, where it was day after day and lasted a couple weeks or more… I can’t really say that.

I may just not be remembering it right, but nothing specific comes to mind. This feels more like the one that stands out.
Before this current period began, did you ever have a time when feeling depressed or losing interest in most things lasted for at least a month?

I don’t think so… not that I can clearly remember.

I mean, a month is a long time, and I’m trying to be careful because I don’t want to just give you an answer because it sounds right. Before this current stretch, I definitely had bad periods — stress, being worn down, maybe a week or a few days where I didn’t feel like myself — but I can’t point to a whole month where I was depressed or lost interest in most things nearly every day.

Nothing like that really stands out before this. This is the one that feels different and more obvious to me.

doctor.intent: Learn the patient's main reason for seeking psychiatric care today
doctor.question: Hi, welcome. What brings you in today?

target_item.name: Loss_of_Interest
target_item.manifestation: I guess the main thing is that I just stopped caring about everything I used to look forward to—my fishing gear is still sitting untouched in the garage, the woodshop feels like a chore, and even when my kids try to get me to play chess I’m just going through the motions.
target_item.reason: This is the first reply of the consultation, so I am returning the chief complaint symptom code as instructed.

patient.answer:
I guess the main thing is… I’ve just kind of stopped caring about everything I used to look forward to. It’s hard to explain without sounding dramatic, but things that used to feel like they were mine, like part of who I was, just don’t pull me in anymore.

Like, I’ve got all my fishing gear still sitting in the garage. Normally I’d be checking it, organizing it, thinking about where to go next, messing with the tackle boxes even when I didn’t have a trip planned. Now I walk past it and it’s like looking at someone else’s stuff. Same with my woodshop. I used to lose hours out there, sanding or cutting or planning some little project, and now even the thought of going out there feels like another chore I’m supposed to do.

And my kids will ask me to play chess, which used to be our thing, and I’ll sit there with them, but I’m not really there. I’m just moving pieces around, going through the motions, trying not to make it obvious that I’m not enjoying it. That’s probably what finally made me feel like I should come in, because it’s not just one thing. It’s like the interest went out of everything.

Most days food just doesn’t really… taste like anything. Cardboard is the word that comes to mind. I’ll know I should eat, especially if I’m going to be on a job site all day, but breakfast is easy for me to just skip now. I used to at least grab something, even if it was quick, but lately I’ll just have coffee or nothing and keep moving.

Dinner’s the same kind of thing. My wife will make food, or there’ll be food there, and I’ll sit down with everyone, but I’m more picking at it than eating. It’s not like I’m trying to diet or lose weight. I just don’t feel like eating, and when I do, it doesn’t feel worth the effort half the time.

And I’ve noticed it physically too. My belt’s had to come in a couple notches, and I didn’t set out for that to happen. I almost didn’t pay attention to it at first, but then you keep using a tighter hole on the belt and it’s kind of hard to pretend it’s nothing.

doctor.intent: Clarify whether there has ever been a prior major depressive episode, which best distinguishes single-episode major depression from recurrent major depression among the leading diagnoses.
doctor.question: Before this started, was there ever a time in your life when you felt depressed or lost interest in almost everything nearly every day for at least two weeks?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about any prior depressive episodes before the current one, but the symptom profile only describes current symptoms and duration, not past history.

patient.answer:
I don’t know that I can point to a clear time like that, no.

I mean, I’ve had rough stretches before — everybody does, I guess — times where work was bad or I was stressed or kind of worn down. But if you’re asking whether there was a period before this where, nearly every day for two weeks or more, I felt depressed or like I lost interest in almost everything… I’m not sure. Nothing is coming to mind that I’d confidently describe that way.

I don’t want to say absolutely never, because memory gets a little fuzzy when you’re trying to compare it to what’s happening now. But I don’t remember anything this persistent or this all-consuming before. This feels different enough that it’s hard for me to match it to some earlier episode.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the depressive syndrome is severe rather than moderate by assessing marked fatigue/loss of energy, a key remaining symptom needed to distinguish the candidate diagnoses.
doctor.question: Have you been feeling tired or like you have very little energy nearly every day?

target_item.name: Fatigue
target_item.manifestation: By midmorning I feel like I’ve already worked a full shift, and even walking the project or climbing stairs with the crew feels like my body is carrying wet concrete.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking directly about feeling tired and having very little energy nearly every day, which matches the Fatigue symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Yeah. Nearly every day, honestly.

It’s not just normal tired, like after a long day on site. It’s more like I wake up already behind. I’ll get going because I have to, but by midmorning I feel like I’ve already worked a full shift. And that’s before the day has really even gotten started.

Walking the project feels harder than it should. Climbing stairs with the crew, going back and forth across the site, even just standing there trying to keep up with what everyone’s saying — my body feels heavy, like I’m carrying wet concrete around with me. That’s the best way I can explain it. Everything takes more effort than it used to.

And I keep trying to tell myself, you know, “Just push through, you’ve done harder days than this,” but it doesn’t feel like the kind of tired that goes away once I get moving. It just kind of sits there all day.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there is significant sleep disturbance, which would help establish whether the patient meets full criteria for a major depressive episode rather than adjustment disorder, and gauge severity among current depressive disorder candidates.
doctor.question: Have you been having trouble sleeping?

target_item.name: Sleep_Disturbance
target_item.manifestation: I can get into bed exhausted, but I either lie there running through bills and schedules or I wake up around three or four in the morning and stare at the ceiling until it’s time to drive to the site.
target_item.reason: The doctor's question directly asks about trouble sleeping, which corresponds to sleep disturbance.

patient.answer:
Yeah. Sleep’s been… pretty bad.

The strange thing is I’ll be exhausted by the time I get into bed, like my body feels completely done, and I’ll think, “Okay, at least I’ll pass out tonight.” But then I lie there and my head just won’t shut off. I’ll start running through bills, schedules, what has to happen on the job site the next day, who’s waiting on what, what I forgot to do, all of that. It’s like as soon as the room gets quiet, everything I’ve been trying not to think about shows up at once.

And if I do fall asleep, a lot of times I’m waking up around three or four in the morning. Not even for a clear reason. I just wake up and stare at the ceiling, and then I’m aware of every minute going by until it’s time to get up and drive to the site. I’ll tell myself not to look at the clock, but then I do, and it just makes it worse.

So yeah, I’m in bed, but I don’t feel like I’m really resting much.

doctor.intent: Assess severity by determining whether the patient has feelings of worthlessness or excessive guilt, which would help distinguish moderate from severe major depressive episode and is more informative now than further probing recurrence.
doctor.question: Have you been feeling worthless?

target_item.name: Worthlessness_Guilt
target_item.manifestation: I keep thinking I’ve failed my wife, my kids, and the guys at work, and if anything goes wrong—a missed appointment, a cost overrun, a safety issue—I take it as proof that I’m useless and everyone would be better off without me in charge.
target_item.reason: The doctor is directly asking about feelings of worthlessness, which matches this symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Yeah… I have. More than I really want to admit.

It’s not like I walk around saying, “I’m worthless,” exactly, but that’s pretty much what it turns into in my head. I keep thinking I’ve failed everybody — my wife, my kids, the guys at work who are counting on me to keep things moving and keep them safe. And then when anything goes wrong, even something that might not totally be on me, I take it like it proves what I already suspect.

Like if I miss an appointment or forget something at home, I’m not just thinking, “Okay, I made a mistake.” I’m thinking, “Of course you did. You can’t even handle basic stuff.” If there’s a cost overrun on a job, or something slips in the schedule, or somebody flags a safety issue, I go straight to, “This is because I’m not good enough to be in charge.” I know construction always has problems — delays, money issues, things you have to solve as they come up — but lately I can’t see it that way. It all feels personal. Like every problem is evidence that I’m useless.

And then I start thinking everyone would probably be better off if I wasn’t the one responsible. My family, the crew, everybody. Not necessarily that they hate me or anything, but just… that I’m letting them down and they’d do better with someone else. It’s hard to say out loud, but yeah, I’ve been feeling pretty worthless.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there have been any periods of elevated or unusually irritable mood suggesting a manic or hypomanic history, which would change the diagnosis away from unipolar depression/adjustment disorder.
doctor.question: Have you ever had a period when you felt unusually up, energized, or irritable compared with your normal self?

target_item.reason: The doctor's question is asking about past periods of unusually elevated, energized, or irritable mood, which relates to manic or hypomanic symptoms. The provided symptom profile only covers depressive symptoms and related impairment/duration, not manic or hypomanic episodes.

patient.answer:
I don’t think so. I mean… not in the way you’re asking, I don’t think.

I’ve had days where I’m wound up or on edge, sure, especially if there’s a lot going on at work or something’s falling apart and I’m trying to keep everyone moving. And I can get irritable, probably more than I should. But unusually up or energized, like I’m suddenly a different person or full of energy compared to normal… no, I can’t really say I’ve had that.

If anything, lately it’s been the opposite. I’m trying to think if there was ever a stretch where I felt kind of unstoppable or like I didn’t need to slow down, and nothing really comes to mind. There are busy periods where you just push because the job demands it, but that feels more like pressure than feeling good or energized. So… no, I haven’t noticed anything like that.

inference.note: Current episode meets criteria for a severe depressive episode: depressed mood/anhedonia for 1 year 7 months with insomnia, low energy, reduced appetite/weight loss, worthlessness, impaired concentration/work functioning, and suicidal ideation. No history suggestive of mania/hypomania. Adjustment disorder is ruled out by full major depressive syndrome and severity; moderate codes are ruled out by suicidality and marked functional impairment. Prior depressive episodes remain unclear, so single vs recurrent cannot yet be distinguished.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there was any prior major depressive episode before the current one to distinguish single-episode major depressive disorder from recurrent major depressive disorder.
doctor.question: Before this current period began, did you ever have a time lasting at least two weeks when you felt depressed or lost interest in most things nearly every day?

target_item.reason: The question asks about any prior depressive episode before the current period, but the provided symptom profile only describes the current episode and its duration, not past episodes.

patient.answer:
I’m… not really sure how to answer that, honestly.

I don’t think I can point to a clear time before this where it was like this for two full weeks, where I was depressed or didn’t care about most things nearly every day. I mean, I’ve had rough stretches, sure — everybody does, I guess — times where work was stressful or I was tired or not myself for a while. But if you’re asking whether there was a definite period before now that felt like this, where it was day after day and lasted a couple weeks or more… I can’t really say that.

I may just not be remembering it right, but nothing specific comes to mind. This feels more like the one that stands out.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there was any prior major depressive episode before the current one, to distinguish recurrent major depressive disorder (F33.2) from single-episode major depressive disorder (F32.2).
doctor.question: Before this current period began, did you ever have a time when feeling depressed or losing interest in most things lasted for at least a month?

target_item.reason: The question asks about any prior depressive or loss-of-interest episode before the current period lasting at least a month, but the symptom profile only covers the current episode and does not include past episodes.

patient.answer:
I don’t think so… not that I can clearly remember.

I mean, a month is a long time, and I’m trying to be careful because I don’t want to just give you an answer because it sounds right. Before this current stretch, I definitely had bad periods — stress, being worn down, maybe a week or a few days where I didn’t feel like myself — but I can’t point to a whole month where I was depressed or lost interest in most things nearly every day.

Nothing like that really stands out before this. This is the one that feels different and more obvious to me.

inference.note: Repeated history suggests no prior depressive episode lasting at least 2 weeks or 1 month before the current 1 year 7 month episode, making recurrent major depressive disorder less likely. Current episode remains severe without psychotic symptoms, with suicidal ideation, anhedonia, insomnia, low appetite/weight loss, fatigue, worthlessness, and occupational impairment; bipolar history denied.

opening_question.question: Hi, welcome. What brings you in today?

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient reports a sustained depressive episode lasting about 1 year and 7 months with pervasive anhedonia, depressed mood most of the time, insomnia, low energy, reduced appetite with weight loss, feelings of worthlessness, impaired concentration/occupational functioning, and recurrent suicidal thoughts including thoughts of steering off the road. He denies any past manic or hypomanic episodes. Although symptoms began in the context of his wife's illness, the severity and breadth of symptoms exceed an adjustment reaction.
